tasks.q: Press Run and watch what happens.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
The words appear on the right, under Program output.
tasks.fb: That is a whole Python program. Run follows your instructions and shows what they display.

teach.say: Python is a language for writing instructions. A computer follows them in order, from the top. print() is the instruction for putting one line on the screen.

lines: Put the word Hello on the screen.

tasks.q: Change the word `"Hello"` to `"Goodbye"`.
brief: Change only the word inside the quotation marks.
Display exactly: Goodbye
tasks.fb: Run and Check are different on purpose. Run is for trying things; Check is for marking.

tests.why: The word Hello is still there. Only the letters inside the quotation marks change.

teach.say: The words inside the quotation marks are yours to choose. Run shows you what your program does. Check my answer compares it with what the task asked for, so Run as often as you like and only Check when you think it is right.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: Three print() instructions give three lines, top to bottom in the order they are written.

teach.say: Python runs the lines in the order they are written, and each print() finishes its line before the next one starts.

tasks.q: Finish the program. Display `"Line one"`. Then display `"Line two"` on the next line.
brief: Line 1 is written for you.
Replace ____ with one instruction of your own.
Display exactly: Line one
Then display exactly: Line two
tasks.fb: Every line of output comes from its own print().

tests.why: Replace the ____ with a print() of your own. It cannot stay there: Python does not know what ____ means.

hint.think: You need the same instruction as line 1, with different words in it.

teach.say: One print() makes one line. A second print() under it makes a second line.

tasks.q: Display the message `"Hello world"`.
brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
Write your program under the line starting with # .
Display exactly: Hello world
Nothing else is displayed.
tasks.fb: You wrote your first program from nothing: print() shows one line, and the quotation marks hold the text.

tests.why: Nothing was displayed. The text goes inside print( ) and inside quotation marks.

hint.think: One instruction, one line of output.

teach.say: This is the first activity with an empty editor. The line already in it starts with a # , which makes it a note to you rather than an instruction: Python ignores it completely. Leave it there and write your program underneath.
code: # This line is a note. Python ignores it.

lines: A note to the person reading the program. Nothing happens when it runs.
Show the words Good morning on the screen.

tasks.q: This program should display `"Ready"`. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and read the error message.
Do not change the word `"Ready"`.
Display exactly: Ready
tasks.fb: Errors are normal and they are useful. NameError means Python was sent looking for a name that does not exist.

tests.why: Text needs a quotation mark at each end. Without them Python hunts for something named Ready and gives up.

hint.think: Python is looking for something named `"Ready"`, because nothing tells it that Ready is text.
walk: Text always has quotation marks round it.
There are two to add, one at each end of the word.

teach.say: An error message is Python saying it could not follow an instruction. Every programmer sees them all day long. Read the last line of the message: it names what went wrong, and the two notes underneath say what to look at.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: Inside quotation marks a digit is just a character to display. Outside them it is a number to work with.

teach.say: Quotation marks change the meaning of what is inside them. With them it is text to show. Without them Python works it out first.

tasks.q: Display `"Line 1 of 2"`. Then display `"Done!"` on the next line.
brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
Display exactly: Line 1 of 2
Then display exactly: Done!
tasks.fb: Inside quotation marks everything is text, so a digit or an exclamation mark is just another character to show.
tasks.starter: # Two lines, digits and punctuation included

tests.why: Copy both lines exactly, the digits and the exclamation mark included.

hint.think: Two lines of output need two instructions.

teach.say: Digits and punctuation inside the quotation marks are part of the text, and print() shows them exactly as written.

tasks.q: Display `"Name: Alex"`. Then display `"Age: 13"` on the next line. Then display `"Town: Bury"` on the next line.
brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
Display exactly: Name: Alex
Then display exactly: Age: 13
Then display exactly: Town: Bury
tasks.fb: Three instructions, three lines, in the order you wrote them.

tests.why: Each line needs its own print(), and the colons are part of the text.

hint.think: Three lines of output, one instruction each.

tasks.q: Display `"Top"`. Then display an empty line. Then display `"Bottom"` on the next line.
brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
Line 1 is `"Top"` and line 3 is `"Bottom"`.
Line 2 has nothing on it at all - not even a space.
tasks.fb: print() with empty brackets gives a blank line, which is how programs are spaced out.

tests.why: A blank line is its own print() with nothing between the brackets. Quotation marks with nothing between them work too.

hint.think: print() can be asked to show nothing at all. What would you put between the brackets?
walk: Line 1 displays `"Top"`.
Line 2 displays nothing.
Line 3 displays `"Bottom"`.

tasks.q: Press Run. The program remembers a number, then shows it.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
score is a name the program made up to remember a value by.
tasks.fb: A variable is a name with a value kept under it. print(score) shows the value, not the word score.

teach.say: A variable lets your program remember something. The name goes on the left of the = sign and the value goes on the right.

lines: Remember the number 10 under the name score.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: Without quotation marks Python shows what the variable holds. With them it shows the letters you typed.

teach.say: Quotation marks round a name turn it into plain text, which is almost never what you want when you are printing a variable.

tasks.q: Change the program so it remembers `25` instead of `10`.
brief: Change only the number.
Display exactly: 25
tasks.fb: Change the value on the right of the = and everything that uses the variable follows.

tests.why: 10 is still being displayed, so the value on the right of the = was not changed.

hint.think: The value a variable holds is the part on the right of the = sign.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it displays what name is holding.
brief: Line 1 is written for you.
Replace ____ with the name of the variable.
Do not put quotation marks round it.
Display exactly: Sam
tasks.fb: print(name) shows the value. print("name") shows the four letters n, a, m, e.

tests.why: If the word name came out, the variable had quotation marks round it. Quotation marks mean show these letters.

hint.think: You want the value, not the letters of the name.

teach.say: To show what a variable holds, put its name inside print() with no quotation marks round it.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: = means put this value in here. The second one replaces the first, and the first is gone.

teach.say: A second = puts a new value in the same variable. The old value is not kept anywhere.

tasks.q: Keep the word `"harbour"` in a variable. Display that variable. Then display it again on the next line.
brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
The word `"harbour"` is written into your program, in one place only.
Display the same variable twice.
tasks.fb: A variable can be used as many times as you like. Writing the word once means there is only one place to change it.
tasks.starter: # Keep a word, then show it twice

tests.why: Both lines come from the same variable, so the word itself is typed once.

hint.think: One variable, two print() instructions.

tasks.q: This program should display `12`. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and read the error message.
Do not change the number.
Display exactly: 12
tasks.fb: SyntaxError means Python could not read the line at all. Here the two sides of the = had been swapped.

tests.why: The two sides of the = are the wrong way round. The name goes on the left.

hint.think: Which side of the = does a name go on?

teach.say: The name always goes on the left of the = and the value on the right. The other way round is not a sentence Python can read.

tasks.q: Keep the word `"north"` in a variable. Display that variable. Then change the variable to the word `"south"`. Display it again on the next line.
brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
Use one variable for both words.
Display the first word before the second one replaces it.
tasks.fb: The order of the lines decides what is displayed. A variable only ever holds one value at a time.
tasks.starter: # One variable, two values, two lines

tests.why: Display the variable before you change it. Once south is in there, north has gone.

hint.think: print() shows the value the variable is holding at that moment.
walk: Put north in the variable.
Display it.
Put south in the same variable.
Display it again.

tasks.q: Keep the word `"amber"` in a variable called `a`. Copy the value of a into a second variable called `b`. Then change a to the word `"silver"`. Display a. Then display b on the next line.
brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
b = a copies the value, so b keeps the word `"amber"`.
Display a first, then b.
tasks.fb: A copy is a copy. b took the value `"amber"` and kept it, whatever happened to a next.
tasks.starter: # Copy a value, then change the original

tests.why: b = a copies the value at that moment. Changing a afterwards does not change b.

hint.think: Copying takes the value out of one variable and puts it in another. The two are not joined afterwards.

tasks.q: Keep the word `"closed"` in a variable. Keep the whole number `100` in a constant called `LIMIT`. Display the variable. Then display `LIMIT` on the next line.
brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
Name the constant `LIMIT`, in capitals.
The number `100` is written into your program in one place only.
tasks.fb: Capitals for a constant tell the next person reading your program that the value is not meant to change.

tests.why: Two values, two names, two lines of output.

hint.think: A constant is made exactly like a variable. Only the name is different.

teach.say: A constant is a value a program never changes once it is set. Python does not stop you changing one, so programmers write the name in capitals as a promise not to.

tasks.q: Press Run. Type a word when the program waits, then press Enter.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
The program stops at input() until something is typed.
tasks.fb: input() is patient: the program sits on that line until the Enter key is pressed.

teach.say: input() stops the program, waits for a line to be typed, and hands that line back. Store what comes back in a variable, or it is thrown away.

lines: Wait for a line to be typed, and keep it under the name word.

tasks.q: The user types Sam. What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: One input() reads one line. The variable then holds it for as long as you need it.

teach.say: Whatever the user types comes back as text, and the variable keeps it until the program changes it.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it keeps what the user types and then displays it.
brief: Replace ____ with a name for the value.
Use the same name that print() already uses.
When you press Check, the words are typed in for you.
Display exactly what was typed, and nothing else.
tasks.fb: input() hands the line back, and the = keeps it under a name you can use later.

tests.why: The name on the left of the = has to match the name inside print().
Whatever the user types comes back, so this works for any word.
input() reads the whole line, spaces included.

hint.think: A value is kept by putting a name and an = in front of it.

teach.say: input() on its own throws the answer away. It has to be put into a variable with an = sign.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Display [word].
brief: The user types in one word.
Keep what comes back in a variable.
[word] means the word that was typed, not the five letters w o r d.
Nothing else is displayed.
tasks.fb: This is the shape of nearly every program you will write: read something, keep it, use it.
tasks.starter: # Read one word, then display it

tests.why: Nothing came out, so the typed word was never displayed.
If the word word came out instead, the variable had quotation marks round it.
input() hands back the whole line, so both words come back as one value.

hint.think: Read the line, keep it, show it. Three jobs, two lines of Python.

teach.say: Square brackets in a task mean a value that changes, not letters to display: [word] means whatever word was typed, so for amber the program displays amber. A message inside input() is shown while the program waits, so the user knows what to type. It is not part of what is marked.

lines: Show Colour? on the screen, wait for a line, and keep it under the name colour.
Show the value colour is holding.

tasks.q: This program should display whatever the user types. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and read the error message.
The user types one word.
Display exactly what was typed.
tasks.fb: NameError here means nothing was ever stored. input() needs a variable in front of it to keep the answer.

tests.why: input() on its own reads the line and throws it away. Nothing called word was ever made.
Give the value a name with an = sign, and use the same name in print().
The name on the left of the = and the name inside print() have to match.

hint.think: Is the answer being kept anywhere? Look at what is missing before the input().

tasks.q: Ask the user for one word. Display [word]. Then display [word] again on the next line. Then display [word] a third time on the next line.
brief: The user types in one word only.
Three lines of output from one word.
tasks.fb: One input() and three print() instructions. Reading a value again would ask the user again.
tasks.starter: # One word in, three lines out

tests.why: Ask once and display the same variable three times.
The whole line comes back, spaces included.
Three print() instructions, one variable.

hint.think: Read it once. A variable can be displayed as many times as you like.

tasks.q: The user types red and then blue. What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: The reading order and the displaying order are separate. The first line typed goes into first, whatever happens next.

teach.say: Each input() reads one line, in the order the lines are typed. The order they are displayed in is up to you.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a second word. Display [second word]. Then display [first word] on the next line.
brief: The user types in two lines, one word on each.
Display the second word first.
tasks.fb: Two values need two names. Reading both into the same variable loses the first one.
tasks.starter: # Two words in, swapped on the way out

tests.why: Use a different variable for each word, or the first one is overwritten.
Read both before displaying either.
The second variable is displayed first.

hint.think: Two words need two variables, or the first is lost when the second arrives.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a second word. Display [first word]. Then display [second word] on the next line. Then display [first word] again on the next line. Then display [second word] again on the next line.
brief: The user types in two lines, one word on each.
Four lines of output from two words.
tasks.fb: Once a value is in a variable it can be used as often as you like, in any order.
tasks.starter: # Two words in, four lines out

tests.why: Two variables, four print() instructions.
Read both words before displaying anything.
The order of the print() lines is the order of the output.

hint.think: Read both words, then display them in the order the task asks for.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word and keep it in its own variable. Then ask for a second word and keep it in its own variable. Then ask for a third word and keep it in its own variable. Display [third word]. Then display [first word] on the next line. Then display [second word] on the next line.
brief: The user types in three lines, one word on each.
Display them in the order the task gives, not the order they were typed.
tasks.fb: The order a program reads values in and the order it displays them in have nothing to do with each other.
tasks.starter: # Three words in, re-ordered on the way out

tests.why: Keep each word in its own variable, then choose the order to display them in.
The third word typed is displayed first.
Read all three before displaying any of them.

hint.think: Three values, three names. Work out which name holds which word before you display anything.

tasks.q: Press Run. The same + sign is used twice and does two different jobs.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
Look at what each line displays, then read the two lines of code again.
tasks.fb: Joining two strings end to end has a name of its own: concatenation.

teach.say: A value's data type decides what can be done with it. 5 is a whole number, or integer. "5" is text, or a string. + adds two numbers, but joins two strings end to end.

lines: 2 and 3 are numbers, so + adds them.
The quotation marks make these strings, so + sticks them together.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: + joins strings exactly as they are, with nothing between them. A space has to be added on purpose.

teach.say: Joining strings does not put a space in for you. If you want one, it has to be in the text.

tasks.q: Change the program so a space appears between the two words.
brief: Keep both variables as they are.
Display exactly: Sam Ali
tasks.fb: " " is a string holding one space. Joining it in the middle puts the gap where you want it.

tests.why: SamAli came out, so nothing was joined between the two words. A space in quotation marks is a string you can join on.

hint.think: A space is a character like any other, so it can go inside quotation marks.

tasks.q: The user types 7. What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: Digits typed in are still text. 7 + 7 would be 14, but "7" + "7" is "77".

teach.say: input() always hands back a string, even when the user typed digits. So + joins rather than adds.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it displays Score: 10.
brief: Replace ____ so the number can be joined to the text.
Display exactly: Score: 10
There is one space after the colon.
tasks.fb: str() makes text out of a number so it can be joined with +.

tests.why: Joining text to a number raises a TypeError. Put the number inside str( ) first.

hint.think: Python will not join text to a number. One of them has to change type.

teach.say: A number cannot be joined to a string with +. str() turns the number into text first, and then it can be joined. There is a second way, which you will see in the syntax reference: print() can be given several values separated by commas, and it puts one space between them. Both are right. This course writes str() and + because then you can see exactly where every space goes.

tasks.q: This program should display Age: 13. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and read the error message.
Do not change the number.
Display exactly: Age: 13
tasks.fb: TypeError means the types do not go together. + needs two strings or two numbers, never one of each.

tests.why: A TypeError here means text and a number were joined with +. Put the number inside str( ).

hint.think: Read the error. What two kinds of value is Python being asked to join?

tasks.q: Ask the user for a town. Then ask for its county. Display the two joined with one space between them.
brief: The user types in two lines, a town on the first and a county on the second.
One line of output.
There is exactly one space between the two.
tasks.fb: Joining strings end to end is called concatenation, and + is the operator that does it.
tasks.starter: # Two words in, one line out

tests.why: Join a space between the two, or they run together.
Both come back as strings, so + joins them.
A town of two words comes back as one whole value.

hint.think: Three strings joined together: the town, a space, and the county.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a colour. Display the line `"The colour is "`[colour].
brief: The user types in one word.
One line of output.
There is one space after is.
tasks.fb: Fixed text plus a value is how nearly every message a program displays is built.
tasks.starter: # Fixed words joined to a typed value

tests.why: Join the fixed text to the variable with +.
Everything before the colour is written into your program.
Whatever is typed comes back whole, spaces included.

hint.think: A fixed piece of text joined to the value the user typed.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Display the word three times on one line, with one space between each one.
brief: The user types in one word.
One line of output, not three.
There is one space between each copy, and none at the start or end.
tasks.fb: A variable can appear as many times as you like in one joined-up string.
tasks.starter: # One word, three times, one line

tests.why: One print() with everything joined inside it, spaces included.
Join the variable to itself with a space string between each copy.
Three copies and two spaces, with nothing on either end.

hint.think: One line of output means one print(). Everything in it has to be joined first.

tasks.q: Press Run. Type 5 when the program waits. Watch what the two lines display.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
Both lines use the number you typed, but they do different things with it.
tasks.fb: int() is what turns the digits the user typed into a number you can do sums with.
tasks.starter:
typed = input("Number? ")
print(typed + typed)
print(int(typed) + int(typed))

teach.say: Casting changes a value from one data type into another. int() makes a whole number out of text, float() makes a decimal, and str() makes text out of a number.

lines: Read a line. It comes back as text, even though it looks like a number.
Join the text to itself, which gives 55.
Turn the text into whole numbers first, so + adds them and gives 10.

tasks.q: The user types 4. What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: int(input()) reads a line and turns it into a number in one go. That is why it appears in so many programs.

teach.say: int() has to be used before the sum, not after it. Once the strings have been joined there is nothing to add.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it adds `1` to the number the user types.
brief: Replace ____ so the typed line becomes a whole number.
The user types one whole number.
Display the number that is one bigger.
tasks.fb: int() round the input() is the standard way to read a number in Python.

tests.why: Without int( ) the + joins the digits instead of adding.
int( ) turns the whole line into one number.
This works for any whole number that is typed.

hint.think: input() hands back text. Something has to turn it into a number.

teach.say: int(input()) is read from the inside out: input() reads the line, and int() turns what came back into a whole number.

tasks.q: This program should display the number that is `10` bigger than the one typed. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and read the error message.
The user types one whole number.
Display one number.
tasks.fb: input() gives text every time. If a value is going to be used in a sum, cast it as it comes in.

tests.why: A TypeError here means a sum was tried on text. Put the input() inside int( ).
Casting has to happen before the sum, not after it.
This works for any whole number once it has been cast.

hint.think: Read the error. input() always hands back text, whatever the user typed.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Work out that number doubled. Display the answer.
brief: The user types one whole number.
One line of output, which is the number multiplied by `2`.
tasks.fb: Read it, work it out, display it. That order is the backbone of almost every program.
tasks.starter: # Read a number, double it, show it

tests.why: Cast the input with int( ) before multiplying.
Zero doubled is zero, which is a useful case to check.
Any whole number works once it has been cast.

hint.think: Read it as a number, work out the answer, display the answer.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: int() cuts the decimal part off. If you want rounding, round() is the one to use.

teach.say: int() on a decimal throws the decimal part away. It does not round to the nearest whole number.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a price with a decimal point in it. Display the line `"The price is "`[price].
brief: The user types one number, which may have a decimal point in it.
Keep it as a decimal number, not a whole number.
One line of output, with one space after is.
tasks.fb: float() for decimals, int() for whole numbers, str() to put a number back into a message.
tasks.starter: # A decimal in, a message out

tests.why: float( ) keeps the decimal part, and str( ) turns it back into text to be joined.
The decimal is kept exactly as it was typed.
A float always displays its decimal part, even when it is zero.

hint.think: A number with a decimal point is a float. Turning it back into text lets it be joined.
start: # now join the message together and display it

tasks.q: Ask the user for their name. Then ask for their age as a whole number. Display the line [name] will be [age plus one] next year.
brief: The user types in two lines: a name, then a whole number.
One line of output.
The age displayed is one more than the age typed.
tasks.fb: Two casts in one program: int() to do the sum, str() to put the answer back into a sentence.
tasks.starter: # A name, an age, and one sentence out

tests.why: Cast the age with int( ) to add to it, and str( ) to join it back into the message.
The full stop at the end is part of the text.
Zero works the same as any other number.

hint.think: The name is text already. The age has to become a number to be added to, then text again to be joined.
walk: Read the name.
Read the age and cast it with int( ).
Add `1` to the age.
Join the whole message together and display it.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display that number on the first line. Then display the same number with a decimal point on the next line. Then display the same number as text joined to itself on the next line.
brief: The user types one whole number.
Line 1 is the number as typed.
Line 2 is the same number as a decimal, so 7 becomes 7.0.
Line 3 is the digits written twice with nothing between them, so 7 becomes 77.
tasks.fb: One value, three types. Casting does not change what the user typed, only how Python treats it.

tests.why: Keep the typed text, then cast it differently for each line.
float( ) adds the .0, and joining the text repeats the digits.
Zero shows the pattern clearly: the text 0 joined to itself is 00.

hint.think: Three data types, one typed value. Which cast gives each one?
walk: Read the line as text and keep it.
Display it as a whole number.
Display it as a float.
Join the text to itself and display that.

tasks.q: The user types 3 and then 4. What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: Read, work out, display. Keeping the answer in its own variable makes the program easier to read.

teach.say: A whole program reads its values, works something out, then displays the answer. That order is called input, process, output.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it displays the two numbers added together.
brief: The user types in two lines, one whole number on each.
Replace ____ with one instruction.
Display one number.
tasks.fb: The reading and casting were done for you. All that was left was the output.

tests.why: Replace the ____ with a print() that adds the two variables.
Both values are already whole numbers, so + adds them.
Zero plus zero is zero.

hint.think: Both numbers are already read and cast. Only the answer is missing.

tasks.q: This program should display the two numbers added together. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and read the error message.
The user types in two lines, one whole number on each.
Display one number.
tasks.fb: A NameError at the end often means the variable was never created, not that it was spelled wrong.
tasks.starter:
a = int(input())
a = int(input())
print(a + b)

tests.why: Both lines were read into a, so nothing called b was ever made.
Give the second value its own name.
Two values, two variables.

hint.think: Look at how many times each variable is read, and which one the second input() goes into.
walk: Two values need two different names.
Reading both into one name loses the first.
Then nothing called `b` exists for the sum.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a whole number. Display the word on the first line. Then display the number doubled on the next line.
brief: The user types in two lines: a word, then a whole number.
Two lines of output.
The second line is the number multiplied by `2`.
tasks.fb: Different values need different data types. Decide the type each one needs before you write the line.
tasks.starter: # A word and a number, each used in its own way

tests.why: Only the number needs int( ). The word is already text.
Zero doubled is zero.
The whole typed line comes back as the word, spaces included.

hint.think: The word stays text. The number has to be cast before it can be doubled.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a name. Then ask for a score as a whole number. Display the line [name] scored [score] points.
brief: The user types in two lines: a name, then a whole number.
One line of output.
There is one space either side of scored, and the word points comes last.
tasks.fb: A message built from fixed text and values is the most common thing a program displays.
tasks.starter: # A name, a score, and one sentence out

tests.why: Put the score inside str( ) so it can be joined to the text.
The full stop at the end is part of the text.
The whole name comes back as one value.

hint.think: Four pieces joined into one string: the name, some fixed text, the score as text, and some more fixed text.
walk: Read the name.
Read the score and cast it with int( ).
Join the four pieces of the message together.
Display the one line.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Then ask for a second whole number. Work out the two numbers added together. Display the line [first] plus [second] is [total].
brief: The user types in two lines, one whole number on each.
One line of output.
There is one space either side of plus and either side of is.
tasks.fb: int() on the way in, str() on the way out. That pattern will come up in every lesson from here.
tasks.starter: # Two numbers in, one sentence out

tests.why: Every number in the message has to go through str( ) to be joined.
The sum uses the numbers; the message uses them as text.
Zeroes show whether the spacing is right.

hint.think: Both numbers are needed as numbers for the sum and as text for the message.
walk: Read both numbers and cast them with int( ).
Work out the total.
Join the five pieces of the message together.
Display the one line.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a name. Then ask for a price with a decimal point. Then ask for a whole number of items. Work out the total cost. Display the line [name] pays [total] for [items] items.
brief: The user types in three lines: a name, a decimal number, then a whole number.
One line of output.
The total is the price multiplied by the number of items.
Display the total exactly as Python gives it, without rounding.
tasks.fb: You have now used every data type in this lesson in one program: a string, a float, an integer and a cast in each direction.
tasks.starter: # Three values, three data types, one sentence

tests.why: float times int gives a float, so the total keeps its decimal part.
Do not round the total: display what Python works out.
Each value needs its own cast on the way in and str( ) on the way out.

hint.think: Three values and three different data types. Work out which cast each one needs.
walk: Read the name as text.
Read the price as a float.
Read the number of items as an int.
Multiply the price by the items.
Join the message together and display it.

stations.name: Final challenge: name the data type

tasks.q: Which data type would Python use for each value?
tasks.fb: Choosing the right type first saves a casting bug later on.

info.title: Start here: how this course works
info.text: Python is a language for writing instructions a computer follows, one line at a time. You write them in the editor on the right of a task window. Run follows your instructions and shows whatever they display in the panel underneath, labelled Program output. Check my answer is different: it marks your program against the task. So run as often as you like while you are trying things out, and check when you think it is right. You can check as many times as you like, and your best mark is the one that is kept. You work through the course in order and complete every question: the next one opens when this one is finished, because each activity teaches what the next one needs. If you are stuck, the Hint button gives you one step at a time, starting with the idea and never with the answer, and Syntax reminder lists every Python command the course has taught so far. I need help is there from the first attempt on every question - it costs you nothing, and it will tell you to ask your teacher and show them the question and your code. Errors are a normal part of programming. Everyone writing Python sees them all day, and reading the message is how you find out what to change. Work round this room through the six numbered badges in order, then tap the star for the final challenge. A badge that says Later is not open yet: finish the one you are on first. Your progress saves after every answer, so you can stop and come back to the same question.

info.title: Naming rules
info.text: A Python variable name can hold letters, digits and underscores, but it cannot start with a digit or contain a space. Capitals are used for the name of a constant, so a reader can see at a glance that the value is not meant to change.

info.title: Why it waits
info.text: input() reads one whole line, so the program only carries on once the Enter key has been pressed. Nothing else happens while it waits.

info.title: One bit each
info.text: A boolean has only two possible values, so it needs just one bit of storage - the smallest piece of data there is.

info.title: Silent rounding
info.text: int() on a float throws the decimal part away instead of rounding, so int(3.9) is 3.

info.title: Reading an error
info.text: A traceback names the line that failed. Read its last line first: that says what Python could not do.
